R-privacy-1 (Addresses with a non-ASCII character escape the mask and are logged in full) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.recommendation: The pattern only matches when the character right before `@` and every character of the domain are ASCII. `logInfo("login failed for josé@exemple.fr")` or `logInfo("signup", { email: "ada@exämple.de" })` match nothing, so the full address reaches the hosting provider's logs, kept 90 days — the very leak the proposal removes (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), Art. 25, Art. 32). Match any non-space, non-`@` run around the `@` (e.g. `[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+`, with the `u` flag) rather than an ASCII allow-list, and add tests with a non-ASCII local part and an internationalized domain.
findings.title: Addresses with a non-ASCII character escape the mask and are logged in full

findings.recommendation: `maskEmails` only recognises a literal `@`. A logged URL or query string such as `logInfo("GET /reset?email=ada%40example.org")` keeps the address in clear, since `%40` is not `@`; e-mail addresses in URLs are a common path into logs. Also match the percent-encoded form (`%40`, case insensitive), or decode before masking, and cover it with a test.
findings.title: URL-encoded addresses (`%40`) are logged in full

findings.recommendation: The mask keeps the first character and the whole domain, so for `a@example.org` the output `a***@example.org` still discloses the complete address — contrary to the logger's own promise that it "never writes a full e-mail address". Keep no character of the local part (e.g. `***@domain`), or at least none when the local part is a single character.
findings.title: A one-letter local part is logged whole

findings.recommendation: First letter plus full domain stays personal data when the domain is small or personal (`j***@dupont-family.fr`), and it is still kept 90 days by the hosting provider. Whether that residual is acceptable depends on the customers' domains, which the review could not see: the team decides whether to also mask the domain or log an opaque identifier instead (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), Art. 25).
findings.title: The masked form still identifies people on personal domains

findings.recommendation: Only field values go through `maskEmails`; a caller that keys fields by address (`logInfo("quota", { [user.email]: 3 })`) would log it in full. No caller exists yet, so this depends on future use: mask the keys too, which costs one call.
findings.title: Field names are not masked
